PraisonAI multiedit writing to persistence locations (authorized_keys / shell rc / cron) AIInstallation High
Hunts the write-side abuse of the GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47 multiedit vulnerability — a Python PraisonAI process writing/modifying files in canonical Linux/Windows persistence locations (~/.ssh/authorized_keys, ~/.bashrc, ~/.bash_profile, ~/.profile, cron, autostart) where no workspace-scoped agent should ever touch. The advisory explicitly calls out writing to ~/.bashrc and ~/.ssh/authorized_keys as the privilege-escalation impact. Rationale: Anchors on the article's Impact section, which explicitly names ~/.bashrc and ~/.ssh/authorized_keys as the privilege-escalation outcomes. Combining the Python+praisonai/multiedit cmdline filter with these specific persistence paths makes this alerting-tier — there is essentially no legitimate scenario where a PraisonAI agent should rewrite a user's shell rc or SSH authorized_keys outside an explicit provisioning playbook.
ATT&CKT1098.004 T1546.004 T1053.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin using PraisonAI as a deliberate Ansible-style provisioner to push authorized_keys to fleet hosts
  • Developer asking PraisonAI to add an alias to their own .bashrc on a personal dev VM
  • Container/cloud-init bootstrap script that happens to embed PraisonAI for initial host config
  • Security researcher reproducing the PoC from the advisory
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "ansible" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "cloud-init")
| where not (DeviceName startswith "dev-" and AccountName == "developer")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Diff the modified file against backup/git history — the inserted content is the payload. Common shapes: a new SSH public key not matching any known engineer fingerprint, a curl|sh trampoline appended to .bashrc, an entry in cron.d calling out to an external URL. Pull the PraisonAI session/prompt that drove the write. Step 2 (contain): Revert the file from backup; if authorized_keys was modified, kill all live SSH sessions for that account and rotate any other access. Disable the agent integration (Telegram/Discord/Slack bot token, API key) and pin praisonai package to >= 4.6.61 across the fleet. Step 3 (hunt): Search 24h forward for SSH logins to this host from any IP whose pubkey matches the freshly-added one; search the org for other hosts where the same praisonai process wrote anywhere outside its workspace.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe", "python3", "python", "python3.exe", "pythonw.exe", "python3.10", "python3.11", "python3.12")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "multiedit")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/.ssh/authorized_keys", "/.bashrc", "/.bash_profile", "/.profile", "/.zshrc", "/etc/cron.d", "/etc/crontab", "/var/spool/cron", "/etc/sudoers", @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\")
   or FileName in~ ("authorized_keys", ".bashrc", ".bash_profile", ".profile", ".zshrc", "crontab", "sudoers")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          PreviousFileName, PreviousFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python", "python3", "pythonw")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "multiedit")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/.ssh/authorized_keys", "/.bashrc", "/.bash_profile", "/.profile", "/.zshrc", "/etc/cron.d", "/etc/crontab", "/var/spool/cron", "/etc/sudoers")
   or TargetFileName in~ ("authorized_keys", ".bashrc", ".bash_profile", ".profile", ".zshrc", "crontab", "sudoers")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable PraisonAI package exposure (< 4.6.61, GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47) AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces hosts running a vulnerable version of the pip:praisonai package so the SOC can drive remediation before exploitation. Pure exposure-management pivot — pairs with the credential-read and persistence detections above so any prior exploitation can be retrospectively hunted on confirmed-vulnerable hosts. Rationale: Targets the exact pip package + version range named in the advisory ('Affected packages: pip:praisonai (vuln < 4.6.61)'). This is the SOC's 'are we even exposed?' query — without it, the hunting detections above have no priority ordering for which hosts to investigate first.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Air-gapped lab hosts where the vulnerable version is intentionally pinned for reproduction research
  • Hosts where Defender TVM has not yet inventoried pip packages (TVM coverage of Python packages is partial — absence does not mean clean)
  • Containers where the praisonai package lives inside an image that TVM cannot introspect
  • Pre-production hosts scheduled for teardown that won't be patched
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Prioritize the result set by IsInternetFacing == true and by chatbot deployment hosts (Telegram/Discord/Slack-integrated PraisonAI is the high-blast-radius shape per the advisory). Step 2 (contain): Drive upgrade to praisonai >= 4.6.61 via the org's pip/Poetry/uv channel; for hosts that can't upgrade immediately, set auto_approve_tools=False on any chatbot integration and remove multiedit from the agent's tool registry. Step 3 (hunt): For every host this query returns, retro-run the credential-read and persistence UCs over the last 90 days — if praisonai was vulnerable, any historical file-access to /etc/shadow or write to authorized_keys by that python process is high-priority IR work, not noise.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has "praisonai" or SoftwareName == "praisonai"
| extend VersionParts = split(SoftwareVersion, ".")
| extend Major = toint(VersionParts[0]), Minor = toint(VersionParts[1]), Patch = toint(VersionParts[2])
| where Major < 4
   or (Major == 4 and Minor < 6)
   or (Major == 4 and Minor == 6 and Patch < 61)
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceInfo
    | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId
    | project DeviceId, IsInternetFacing, MachineGroup, LoggedOnUsers
  ) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion,
          OSPlatform, IsInternetFacing, MachineGroup, LoggedOnUsers
| order by tostring(IsInternetFacing) desc, DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SoftwareName has "praisonai"
| extend VersionParts = split(SoftwareVersion, ".")
| extend Major = toint(VersionParts[0]), Minor = toint(VersionParts[1]), Patch = toint(VersionParts[2])
| where Major < 4
   or (Major == 4 and Minor < 6)
   or (Major == 4 and Minor == 6 and Patch < 61)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel
| order by DeviceName asc

Unauthenticated JSON-RPC tools/call hitting an internal MCP HTTP listener AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP POST traffic carrying JSON-RPC method strings ('tools/call','tools/list','resources/read','prompts/get') against the MCP server's default listener port. Targets the specific exploit shape from GHSA-j4f3-55x4-r6q2 where the praisonai TypeScript MCPServer accepts these methods with no Authorization check and binds to all interfaces. Rationale: Anchors on the article's two strongest fingerprints: (1) the specific JSON-RPC method strings handleRequest() dispatches without auth ('tools/call','tools/list','resources/read','prompts/get','initialize'), and (2) the default port 3000 + node.exe parent process running praisonai/mcp/server code. The Sentinel query also captures the article's PoV confirming 'Bearer invalid' is ignored — a Bearer-invalid POST that returns 200 is decisive.
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal MCP clients on the same host invoking tools/list against a development instance
  • Security scanners (Nuclei, Burp, internal pentest) probing JSON-RPC endpoints on port 3000
  • Loopback PoV/PoC runs by the developer hardening their MCP server
  • Other JSON-RPC services on port 3000 unrelated to praisonai (e.g. Ethereum-style RPC, internal dashboards)
  • Health-check / monitoring probes that send empty POST bodies
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("--test", "--scan", "NODE_ENV=development") | where RemoteIP !in (vuln_scanner_ips) | where AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull the offending host's praisonai version (`npm ls praisonai`) and confirm MCPServer.start() is called with HTTP transport; review the WAF/proxy log around the alert window for the source IP, JSON-RPC method, and whether Authorization header was present/valid. Step 2 (contain): if the listener is reachable from outside the trust boundary, block inbound 3000 at the host firewall, restart the node process bound to 127.0.0.1, or stop the service until a patched version (post-1.7.1 with auth wired) is deployed. Step 3 (hunt): for the same source IP, search EmailEvents and DeviceProcessEvents for follow-on activity — node.exe spawning cmd/powershell/bash (tool handler abuse), unexpected file writes by node.exe, and DNS/outbound from the node process to non-corp domains within 1 hour of the inbound JSON-RPC.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort == 3000
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "praisonai-ts", "mcp/server", "MCPServer")
| where RemoteIPType !in ("Loopback", "Private") or RemoteIP !in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteIPType, LocalIP, LocalPort,
          InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 3000
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where Message has_any ('"method":"tools/call"', '"method":"tools/list"', '"method":"resources/read"', '"method":"prompts/get"', '"method":"initialize"')
| extend AuthHeaderPresent = Message has "Authorization:"
| extend AuthInvalid = Message has_cs "Authorization: Bearer invalid" or Message matches regex @"(?i)Authorization:\s*Bearer\s+(invalid|test|null|undefined)\b"
| where not(AuthHeaderPresent) or AuthInvalid
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort,
          RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, AuthHeaderPresent, AuthInvalid, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationPort:3000 (@Image:(*\node.exe OR *\Node.exe OR *\NODE.EXE)) -CIDR(@SourceIp, 127.0.0.0/8) -CIDR(@SourceIp, ::1/128)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 LocalPort=3000 ConnectionDirection="1" ContextImageFileName=/node\.exe$/i | regex("(praisonai|MCPServer|mcp/server)", field=ContextImageFileName, strict=false) OR join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/node\.exe$/i CommandLine=/praisonai|MCPServer|mcp\/server/i | groupBy([aid, TargetProcessId])}, field=[aid, ContextProcessId]) | NOT cidr("127.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4, LocalPort, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

Vulnerable praisonai npm package (<=1.7.1) installed on host AIWeaponization High
Detects the on-disk fingerprint of the vulnerable npm package (`node_modules/praisonai/package.json` and the unguarded `src/praisonai-ts/src/mcp/server.ts` file) being written during `npm install`. Treat as a hunting hook to find every machine that needs patching before the wider attack-surface hunt. Rationale: Targets the exact file artefacts named in the article ('src/praisonai-ts/src/mcp/server.ts' and the npm package layout). Combining 'node_modules/praisonai' with an npm/yarn/pnpm parent eliminates source-checkout false positives. Pairs with UC1 — patch the hosts this lights up before UC1 trips for real.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer machines doing legitimate development against the praisonai source tree (not exposed to network)
  • CI build runners installing dependencies in ephemeral containers for testing
  • Security-research/sandbox VMs deliberately installing the vulnerable version for reproduction
  • Mirror/cache servers (Verdaccio, Artifactory) pre-fetching the package
  • Old development branches resurrected during git checkout that contain the package.json on disk but never serve it
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Users\\" | where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\" | where DeviceName !in (dev_workstations_watchlist)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): for each host, capture `node_modules/praisonai/package.json` `version` and `dependencies`; confirm whether the host runs `MCPServer.start({port:...})` in production code (grep repo for `MCPServer` instantiation). Step 2 (contain): if production, force-upgrade to a patched version once published or pin to a fork that wires MCPSecurity into startHttp() and binds to 127.0.0.1; in the interim, add a host-firewall rule blocking inbound 3000 from non-loopback. Step 3 (hunt): for every host that has the file, pivot to UC1 over the last 30 days to check whether anyone has already exploited it; pull `node.exe` outbound DNS and process-tree for the same window.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has "node_modules\\praisonai" or FolderPath has "node_modules/praisonai" or FolderPath has "praisonai-ts\\src\\mcp" or FolderPath has "praisonai-ts/src/mcp"
| where FileName in~ ("package.json", "server.ts", "server.js")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe", "npm-cli.js", "node.exe", "pnpm.exe", "yarn.exe", "corepack.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType =~ "FileCreated" or EventType =~ "FileRenamed"
| where TargetFilePath has "node_modules/praisonai" or TargetFilePath has "node_modules\\praisonai" or TargetFilePath has "praisonai-ts/src/mcp" or TargetFilePath has "praisonai-ts\\src\\mcp"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("package.json", "server.ts", "server.js")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("npm", "node", "pnpm", "yarn", "corepack")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node.js praisonai MCP server spawning shell or scripting interpreter (tool-call abuse) AIActions on Objectives High
Post-exploitation pivot: an unauthenticated tools/call from UC1 lets the attacker invoke whatever tool handlers the MCPServer registered. Many handlers wrap shell, file, or db actions. This catches node.exe (with praisonai in its cmdline) spawning cmd/powershell/bash/sh as a child — the most common abuse shape regardless of which specific tool is registered. Rationale: The article notes 'MCP tools commonly wrap filesystem operations, API clients, database queries, agent actions, deployment operations, email/Slack actions, browser automation, and code execution'. A node.exe parent whose cmdline references praisonai/MCPServer spawning a shell or scripting interpreter is the single highest-fidelity post-exploit signature regardless of which tool was registered, and pairs cleanly with UC1 as the network-side trigger.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.003 T1059.004 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate registered MCP tools that genuinely wrap shell commands (e.g. a 'run_terminal' tool) used by the application's own AI agent loop
  • Developer testing the MCPServer locally with example tools that exec shell
  • npm postinstall scripts running during package upgrade (node spawning shell briefly)
  • CI/CD pipelines using praisonai for build-step orchestration that legitimately spawn shells
  • Application healthcheck/monitoring scripts invoked by node parent
Suppression filter
| where ChildCmd !has_any ("npm install", "npm run", "node-gyp", "yarn install") | where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("npm.exe", "yarn.exe", "pnpm.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): grab the child process commandline, hash, and any spawned descendants — confirm whether the action looks like a registered MCP tool's legitimate work or arbitrary attacker input (recon strings, encoded payloads, outbound network from the child). Pull the inbound JSON-RPC request from UC1 in the same minute. Step 2 (contain): isolate the host (or stop the node MCP service), revoke any credentials accessible to the node process (env vars, IAM role, .aws/credentials, .npmrc tokens). Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the child's outbound DNS/IPs and any file writes for next-stage payloads; check the source IP of the UC1 request against threat intel and enumerate every other host running praisonai (UC2) for the same source-IP probes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "praisonai-ts", "MCPServer", "mcp/server", "mcp\\server")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "bash.exe", "wsl.exe", "sh.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "mshta.exe", "curl.exe", "certutil.exe", "bitsadmin.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "node" or ParentProcessName endswith "node.exe"
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "praisonai-ts", "MCPServer", "mcp/server", "mcp\\server")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "bash", "sh", "wsl.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "mshta.exe", "curl.exe", "certutil.exe")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, Hash
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.

Vulnerable PraisonAI npm AgentOS server process running (GHSA-9752-mhqh-h34f, 1.6.0-1.7.1) AIInstallation High
Inventory hunt for Node processes running the npm `praisonai` AgentOS HTTP server. Per GHSA-9752-mhqh-h34f, versions 1.6.0-1.7.1 register `/api/agents` and `/api/chat` without any auth middleware and default-bind to 0.0.0.0, so any running instance is a candidate for unauthenticated agent invocation. Surfaces all hosts running the vulnerable component so they can be loopback-bound, patched, or fronted with auth before exploitation. Rationale: Anchored on the exact strings the advisory cites — package name `praisonai`, the shipped artifact path `dist/os/agentos.js`, and the Node host runtime — none of which appear in benign Node command lines. Cross-referenced the Python/PyPI sibling advisories (GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj, CVE-2026-44338) which confirm the same /api/agents + /api/chat unauthenticated shape and prove this class of bug is being actively exploited within hours of disclosure. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/MervinPraison/PraisonAI/security/advisories/GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/praisonai-cve-2026-44338-auth-bypass.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/praisonai-vulnerability-exploited/
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer laptops with praisonai installed for local evaluation (host arg explicitly set to 127.0.0.1)
  • CI/CD runners executing praisonai integration tests in ephemeral containers
  • Sanctioned internal AgentOS deployments already behind an auth-enforcing reverse proxy (nginx/Traefik with bearer-token middleware)
  • Security-research lab hosts running the GHSA PoV reproduction
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("jest.exe", "node-test-runner.exe") and AccountName !endswith "$" and not (DeviceName matches regex "(?i)(dev|build|ci|runner|sandbox)-")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm running praisonai version (`npm ls praisonai` in the install root) and the bind address — run `netstat -ano | findstr 8000` (Win) or `ss -ltnp | grep node` (Linux) to determine whether the listener is on 0.0.0.0 or 127.0.0.1. Check internet exposure via external IP scan / asset inventory. 2) CONTAIN: If bound to 0.0.0.0 with no upstream auth, immediately stop the service, restart with `host: '127.0.0.1'`, or place behind a reverse proxy enforcing a bearer token; if internet-exposed, block port at the edge firewall first. 3) HUNT: Pivot to web/proxy logs for `/api/agents` and `/api/chat` requests over the prior 30 days from any non-loopback source — any hit before the listener was rebound is presumptive compromise; review what tools (file/MCP/credential) the configured agent had reachable.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe", "node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "agentos.js", "dist/os/agentos", @"dist\os\agentos", "AgentOS")
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            arg_max(Timestamp, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, AccountName)
        by DeviceId, DeviceName
| project DeviceName, AccountName, FirstSeen, LastSeen, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by LastSeen desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\node.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "/node"
| where CommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "agentos.js", "dist/os/agentos", @"dist\os\agentos", "AgentOS")
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            arg_max(TimeGenerated, CommandLine, NewProcessName, SubjectUserName)
        by Computer
| project Computer, SubjectUserName, FirstSeen, LastSeen, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by LastSeen desc
title: PraisonAI Vulnerable npm AgentOS Server Execution (GHSA-9752-mhqh-h34f)
id: 9752a8b2-mhqh-4e2f-9a1b-h34f00000001
status: experimental
description: Detects execution of the Node-based npm praisonai AgentOS HTTP server. Versions 1.6.0-1.7.1 expose /api/agents and /api/chat without authentication and default-bind to 0.0.0.0.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9752-mhqh-h34f
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1133
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_image:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '/node'
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'praisonai'
      - 'agentos.js'
      - 'dist/os/agentos'
      - 'dist\os\agentos'
  condition: selection_image and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
  - Developer workstations evaluating praisonai
  - CI/CD pipelines running praisonai integration tests
  - Sanctioned internal AgentOS deployments fronted by an authenticated reverse proxy
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:*\node.exe OR @Image:*\NODE.EXE OR @Image:*\Node.exe OR @Image:*/node) AND (@CommandLine:*praisonai* OR @CommandLine:*PraisonAI* OR @CommandLine:*agentos.js* OR @CommandLine:*AgentOS*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\node(\.exe)?$/i
| regex("(praisonai|agentos\\.js|dist[\\\\/]os[\\\\/]agentos|AgentOS)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="node.exe" OR Processes.process_name="node") AND (Processes.process="*praisonai*" OR Processes.process="*agentos.js*" OR Processes.process="*dist/os/agentos*" OR Processes.process="*dist\\os\\agentos*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process Processes.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | eval ghsa="GHSA-9752-mhqh-h34f"
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="node.exe" OR Processes.process_name="node") AND (Processes.process="*praisonai*" OR Processes.process="*agentos.js*" OR Processes.process="*dist/os/agentos*" OR Processes.process="*dist\\os\\agentos*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process Processes.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | eval ghsa="GHSA-9752-mhqh-h34f"
Unauthenticated request to PraisonAI AgentOS /api/agents or /api/chat from non-loopback source AIExploitation High
Detects HTTP requests to the AgentOS endpoints `/api/agents` (GET — agent enumeration) or `/api/chat` (POST — agent invocation) from a non-loopback source with no `Authorization` header. Per GHSA-9752-mhqh-h34f, these routes are registered with zero auth middleware in npm praisonai 1.6.0-1.7.1, so any such request from a non-loopback IP is presumptive exploitation of the missing authentication boundary. Rationale: Targets the exact two routes the advisory names — `/api/agents` (line 235 of `agentos.ts`) and `/api/chat` (line 250) — gated on (a) source not being loopback and (b) absent Authorization header, which together exactly reproduce the PoV's vulnerable-request shape and the patched 401 control. Cross-referenced the live exploitation pattern reported in the PyPI sibling write-ups, where the same two routes were targeted within hours of disclosure. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/MervinPraison/PraisonAI/security/advisories/GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj • https://gbhackers.com/praisonai-vulnerability-actively-exploited/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/praisonai-cve-2026-44338-auth-bypass.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal load balancer / reverse proxy health probes hitting `/api/agents` (real proxy IP, no auth header)
  • Developer making local-LAN curl requests for testing (non-loopback but trusted)
  • Sanctioned internal monitoring (Datadog/Prometheus blackbox exporters) calling `/api/agents` for liveness
  • Sibling-service polling in a Docker network where source IP is the bridge gateway, not loopback
  • Pen-test or vuln-scanner traffic during scheduled internal assessment
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in (<trusted_LB_IPs>) and SrcIpAddr !startswith "10." and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has_any ("kube-probe", "GoogleHC", "ELB-HealthChecker", "Datadog Agent", "blackbox_exporter")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the source IP — is it internal/trusted (LB, monitoring agent, dev workstation) or external/unknown? Pull the full `/api/chat` request body to see the prompt that was sent — that prompt IS the attacker's command to the agent. Capture HTTP response too: 200 means the agent ran. 2) CONTAIN: Block source IP at the edge, stop the AgentOS service or restart with `host: '127.0.0.1'` and an `Authorization` middleware shim, and revoke any credentials/API keys present in the AgentOS process environment that the invoked agent could have reached. 3) HUNT: For every `/api/chat` POST you confirm, enumerate the configured agent's tools (file/MCP/HTTP/credential tools) and pull their telemetry for the same window — outbound network from the Node PID, files written by the agent, downstream API calls — to scope what the prompt-injected agent actually did.
let praisonHosts = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName in~ ("node.exe", "node")
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "agentos.js", "dist/os/agentos")
    | summarize by DeviceId, DeviceName;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe", "node")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "agentos.js", "dist/os/agentos")
| where LocalPort in (8000, 3000, 4000)
| where RemoteIPType != "Loopback"
| join kind=inner praisonHosts on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteIPType, RemotePort, LocalPort,
          InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackHours = 24h;
let AgentOSPorts = dynamic([8000, 3000, 4000, 80, 443]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
| where Url has_any ("/api/agents", "/api/chat")
| where HttpMethod in~ ("GET", "POST")
| where DstPortNumber in (AgentOSPorts) or isempty(DstPortNumber)
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1", "::1", "0.0.0.0")
| extend EndpointHit = case(Url has "/api/agents", "agents",
                            Url has "/api/chat", "chat", "other")
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            Hits = count(), HitMethods = make_set(HttpMethod, 10),
            HitUrls = make_set(Url, 20), Endpoints = make_set(EndpointHit, 5),
            HitStatuses = make_set(HttpStatusCode, 10)
        by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, DstIpAddr
| project FirstSeen, LastSeen, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, DstIpAddr, Hits, Endpoints, HitMethods, HitUrls, HitStatuses
| order by FirstSeen desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ConnectionDirection=0
| (LocalPort=8000 OR LocalPort=3000 OR LocalPort=4000)
| ContextImageFileName=/\\node(\.exe)?$/i
| regex("(praisonai|agentos\\.js|dist[\\\\/]os[\\\\/]agentos)", field=ContextImageFileName)
| NOT (RemoteAddressIP4=/^127\./)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4, LocalPort, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
| _count > 0

Node.js spawning shell with reconnaissance commands (PraisonAI codeMode sandbox escape) AIExploitation High
Detects node/node.exe spawning sh/bash/cmd/powershell that immediately runs reconnaissance commands (whoami, uname, /etc/passwd, ~/.ssh). This is the post-RCE primitive demonstrated in the GHSA-p69m-4f92-2v84 PoC where `cp.execSync('id')` was used to confirm sandbox escape via `Function('return this')()` + `global.require('child_'+'process')`. Catches exploitation of any JS sandbox-escape pattern that ends in child_process invocation, not just PraisonAI. Rationale: The GHSA's PoC explicitly demonstrates RCE via `cp.execSync('id').toString()` after escaping the sandbox with `Function('return this')()` and `global.require('child_'+'process')`. Whatever the attacker prompt-injects into `codeMode`, the deterministic OS-level signal is the same: node spawns a shell (Node child_process always exec's via /bin/sh or cmd.exe), and the spawned shell runs recon. Pairing parent=node with child=shell with a recon-command cmdline gives high fidelity because legitimate Node apps rarely shell out to enumerate /etc/passwd or ~/.ssh. I did not web-search — this is a fresh advisory (published <30 days) with no expected secondary corroboration yet.
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.003 T1082 T1033 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node-based CI/CD agents (Jenkins agents, GitHub Actions runners, GitLab runners written in Node) executing pipeline scripts that call hostname/whoami for build metadata
  • Node.js diagnostic / health-check libraries (e.g. systeminformation, node-os-utils) shelling out to ifconfig or uname for system info
  • Containerized Node services running an entrypoint script that prints hostname/whoami at startup for logging
  • npm postinstall scripts that probe the environment (e.g. node-gyp builds detecting kernel version with uname -r)
  • Developer-machine Node REPL sessions where engineers manually run cp.execSync('whoami') for testing
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp", "node-pre-gyp", "systeminformation", "node-os-utils", "/actions-runner/", "/gitlab-runner/", "/jenkins/") or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"^(?:/bin/sh|/bin/bash)\s+-c\s+\"?hostname\"?\s*$")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the parent Node command line (InitiatingProcessCommandLine) and the script that was being executed. Look for `praisonai`, `codeMode`, `new Function(`, `with (sandbox)`, or `Function('return this')` in process args, loaded scripts, or recent npm package.json on the host. Check the spawning Node process's exposure — is it an LLM-agent backend reachable from the internet? Step 2 — Contain: if praisonai-ts <=1.7.1 is installed and the Node process is internet-exposed, stop the service, snapshot the host, and rotate any credentials in the process environment (env-var API keys are the GHSA's stated impact). Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the same DeviceId for (a) DeviceFileEvents to /tmp, /var/tmp, ~/.ssh, or .bashrc by node; (b) DeviceNetworkEvents from the node ProcessId to public IPs (exfil/C2); (c) DeviceProcessEvents for follow-on curl/wget/bash -i invocations spawned in the same logon session.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe", "node")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\b(whoami|uname|hostname|ifconfig)\b"
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd", "/etc/shadow", "~/.ssh", "/root/.ssh", "ip addr", "cat /root/", "id;", "id |", "id&&")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "code-mode", "codeMode", "new Function", "Function('return this')") 
   or AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256, ProcessId, InitiatingProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\node.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "/node"
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\cmd.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\pwsh.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "/sh" or NewProcessName endswith "/bash" or NewProcessName endswith "/dash" or NewProcessName endswith "/zsh"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\b(whoami|uname|hostname|ifconfig)\b"
   or CommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd", "/etc/shadow", "~/.ssh", "/root/.ssh", "ip addr", "cat /root/")
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, NewProcessId, ProcessId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable PraisonAI-TS package (<=1.7.1) installed — GHSA-p69m-4f92-2v84 AIWeaponization High
Hunts for hosts with the npm package `praisonai` (or `praisonai-ts`) at a version <=1.7.1 installed, which is vulnerable to the codeMode tool sandbox-escape RCE. Catches at-risk inventory before exploitation. Pivots on TVM software inventory and on file-event evidence of the package directory. Rationale: The GHSA names the exact vulnerable package and ceiling (`praisonai <=1.7.1`) and the exact file path (`src/praisonai-ts/src/tools/builtins/code-mode.ts`). DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory gives clean inventory for hosts where the package is registered; the DeviceFileEvents fallback catches hand-installed copies or container-baked images that TVM may not enumerate. Sentinel KQL is empty because the analyst-tenant Sentinel schema in this environment does not expose DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory or a file-event table covering node_modules paths — operators should hunt this via Defender XDR or the npm-audit pipeline. CloudWatch is empty for the same reason (not AWS telemetry).
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Inventory.Software
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal security-research/test hosts deliberately running the vulnerable version to validate detections — keep but tag
  • Developer workstations with the package in a sandboxed test directory unrelated to production services
  • Container build hosts where the image is built but never executed in production (pre-bake CI runners)
  • Vendored copies inside another repo (node_modules of a different project that depends on praisonai transitively but isn't internet-exposed)
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sec-research-", "detection-lab-", "-buildagent-") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("docker.exe", "containerd-shim.exe", "buildkitd"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: for each hit, determine whether the host is internet-exposed and whether the praisonai agent is actually instantiated with `codeMode` enabled (grep the host's app config for `code-mode`, `codeMode`, or `tools: [codeMode]`). If codeMode is not enabled, downgrade to advisory; the vulnerable code path requires the tool to be wired into an agent. Step 2 — Contain: for exposed services with codeMode enabled, force-pin the dependency to a patched version (>=1.7.2 once published) or disable the codeMode tool in agent config; rotate any API keys/secrets present in the Node process environment. Step 3 — Hunt: cross-reference hit hosts against UC #1 (Node spawning shell with recon) over the past 30d to confirm no prior exploitation. Add the package directory to a watch-list for change events (new versions, new installs) until the org-wide upgrade is complete.

let vuln = DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
  | where SoftwareName has "praisonai"
  | where SoftwareVersion matches regex @"^(0\.|1\.[0-6]\.|1\.7\.[01](?:$|[^0-9]))"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion;
// Filesystem fallback — catches manual / non-managed installs TVM missed
let fileEvidence = DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)node_modules[\\/]praisonai(?:-ts)?[\\/]"
  | where FileName =~ "package.json"
  | summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Paths=make_set(FolderPath, 25) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName;
union isfuzzy=true vuln, fileEvidence
| order by DeviceName asc

Node.js spawned shell/utility from praisonai codeMode context (sandbox escape post-exploitation) AIExploitation High
Hunts for Node.js processes that load the praisonai package (which advertises codeMode as a sandbox) but then spawn child shell/utility processes. A working sandbox would not permit child_process.spawn; any such child indicates the Function-constructor / prototype-chain escape described in GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp succeeded. Rationale: Pivots on the article's named package string 'praisonai' and the tool name 'codeMode' (src/praisonai-ts/src/tools/builtins/code-mode.ts) appearing in the node parent process command line, combined with shells/utilities the codeMode blocklist explicitly forbids — printf was the exact binary spawned in the published PoV. Cross-checked GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp advisory page; npmjs praisonai package listing. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp • https://www.npmjs.com/package/praisonai
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1068 T1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running praisonai dev/test scripts that legitimately use shell tooling outside codeMode
  • CI/CD jobs invoking praisonai e2e tests that intentionally spawn child processes
  • Postinstall hooks of @praisonai dev tooling using node to call printf for logging
  • Maintainer reproduction of the PoV (poc/pov_poc.js) on a research host
  • Containerised praisonai workloads using shell-invoking node tools (langchain.js shell tool, etc.)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("test","jest","vitest","mocha","npm run test","e2e") and AccountName has_any ("dev","build","ci","jenkins"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull full process tree on the host — confirm the parent node.exe has praisonai/code-mode in cmdline and identify whether the child shell ran an attacker-supplied command (look for env-var dumps, file reads, or outbound network). 2) Contain: isolate the host via Defender Live Response, kill the offending node.exe PID, snapshot /tmp + cwd of the node process, rotate any secrets exposed via process.env (cloud API keys, LLM provider tokens). 3) Hunt: search 30d for the same node + praisonai parent → child shell pattern on other hosts; pivot on any DeviceFileEvents writes by node.exe to non-project paths and on outbound network from node.exe to non-LLM-provider IPs (post-escape egress).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","code-mode","codeMode")

id: 6f5b0c52-1c3e-4d51-8b1a-3a7b7c2d8e91
description: Detects child shell or scripting processes spawned by node.exe whose command line indicates praisonai/codeMode is loaded. The codeMode tool advertises a sandbox boundary and explicitly blocks child_process; any spawned shell child is evidence of GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp prototype-chain escape.
references:
    - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/18

PraisonAI codeMode prototype-chain escape payload (constructor.constructor / mainModule.require strings) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts for the literal prototype-chain escape strings from the GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp PoV — '({}).constructor.constructor', 'return process', and 'process.mainModule.require' — appearing in node.exe command lines, AMSI-captured scripts, or files written under node_modules/praisonai. These strings are the exact bypass used to defeat codeMode's regex blocklist. Rationale: Anchors on the exact strings the advisory and PoV publish — '({}).constructor.constructor', 'process.mainModule.require', and the 'return process' inner Function body. These are the specific bypass primitives proven to defeat codeMode's blocklist (lines 108-113 of code-mode.ts) and would not appear in benign node.exe command lines or production praisonai usage. Cross-referenced against GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp and the praisonai npm package source. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp • https://www.npmjs.com/package/praisonai
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1027 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher running the published PoV (poc/pov_poc.js) on a known sandbox/research host
  • Node.js sandbox-escape educational material executed in a dev environment
  • Internal red-team exercise validating the GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp finding
  • Unit tests in vm2/isolated-vm wrapper libraries that intentionally test prototype-chain bypasses
  • Sigma/Yara rule self-test where rule strings appear inside test corpora
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full node.exe command line and grandparent process — confirm whether this is the published PoV (poc/pov_poc.js) on a research host, or a production praisonai deployment receiving attacker-controlled tool input. 2) Contain: if production, isolate the host and force-uninstall praisonai pending upgrade past GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp fix; rotate any secrets reachable via process.env on that host. 3) Hunt: search DeviceFileEvents 30d for praisonai package installs across the fleet (node_modules/praisonai/dist/tools/builtins/code-mode.js), enumerate which versions are present, and correlate with any node.exe → shell spawns from UC1 to identify successful exploitations.

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Salesforce REST API mass /sobjects enumeration via OAuth connected app
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound/SaaS connections to Icarus extortion group IPs (Klue/Salesforce campaign) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Klue Battlecards connected app Salesforce activity from Icarus IPs · [LLM] Salesforce /query API burst exfiltration via single OAuth principal · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Outbound/SaaS connections to Icarus extortion group IPs (Klue/Salesforce campaign) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts traffic to/from the four IP addresses ReliaQuest and Huntress attributed to the Icarus actors who stole Salesforce CRM data via the Klue Battlecards OAuth breach. Catches both endpoint-level connections and any Salesforce/SaaS sign-in or API call sourced from those IPs. Rationale: Four IPs are explicitly attributed by both ReliaQuest and Huntress in the article and corroborated by their independent blog posts. Cross-platform pivot because Icarus is reaching Salesforce/AAD via OAuth, not just endpoints, so identity-plane sign-ins matter as much as network egress. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-integration-abused-in-crm-data-theft • https://www.huntress.com/blog/klue-breach-investigation • https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/salesforce-data-thefts-klue-app-compromise • https://status.salesforce.com/generalmessages/20000257
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web Authentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel platforms or sandboxes legitimately fetching these IPs for enrichment
  • Security researchers running their own analysis of the Icarus infrastructure
  • Shared NAT egress IP collisions on residential ISP ranges hosting unrelated SaaS users
  • SOC analyst manual reproduction during incident triage
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("threatintel","soc-analyst"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: For each hit identify the principal (user, service principal, or Klue Battlecards connected app) and confirm whether the activity touched Salesforce APIs or other SaaS. Check whether the workstation is in the security team's analysis fleet. 2) Contain: Revoke any OAuth refresh tokens for the involved user/service principal, force-rotate Salesforce session tokens, terminate active sessions, and add the four IPs to perimeter blocklists if not already. Block the Klue Battlecards connected app at the Salesforce tenant level. 3) Hunt: Pivot to 30 days of Salesforce REST API activity from the same connected app or user looking for `/services/data/v59.0/sobjects` enumeration or `/services/data/v59.0/query` bursts; check for similar OAuth-app activity from any of the four IPs across other SaaS integrations (HubSpot, SharePoint, Slack, Google Drive that Klue also integrates with).

Klue Battlecards connected app Salesforce activity from Icarus IPs AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts Salesforce API activity attributed to the Klue Battlecards OAuth connected app sourced from the four IPs that ReliaQuest/Huntress tied to the Icarus actor. The combination of the Klue connected-app identifier with any of those IPs is essentially a confirmed-compromise signal during this incident. Rationale: Combines the article's named compromised connected app (Klue Battlecards) with the four Icarus IPs that ReliaQuest and Huntress independently published. Per Huntress, the Klue dormant prototype credential generated tokens — so service-principal-style sign-ins are the right pivot, not just interactive user logons. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-integration-abused-in-crm-data-theft • https://www.huntress.com/blog/klue-breach-investigation • https://www.salesforceben.com/another-oauth-hack-salesforce-disables-third-party-app-as-crm-data-exposed-again/
ATT&CKT1528 T1199 T1530
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Salesforce admin investigating the incident from a customer IP coincidentally in the range
  • Klue support staff legitimately accessing tenant config during incident response (should appear as Salesforce-side admin, not connected-app token)
  • Tenant that already disabled the Klue Battlecards app and is seeing residual failed sign-in attempts (still worth alerting as recon)
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm whether the tenant ever had Klue Battlecards installed and whether Salesforce has already revoked the connected app per its 2026-06-17 trust advisory. Pull the full Salesforce Event Monitoring log for the connected-app principal in the 24h preceding the alert. 2) Contain: Revoke all OAuth refresh tokens for the Klue connected app, terminate all sessions, force-rotate any service-account credentials Klue held, and explicitly remove the Klue Battlecards installed package. Disable the four IPs at the IDP/CASB. 3) Hunt: List every SObject the connected-app principal queried in the past 30 days (this maps directly to what data was exfiltrated). Pivot for the same OAuth client_id hitting non-Salesforce SaaS that Klue integrated with (HubSpot, SharePoint, Zoom, Gong, Chorus, Clari, Google Drive, Slack) — Klue disabled those integrations per Huntress, so any post-disablement activity is a strong tell.
let IcarusIPs = dynamic(["138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160"]);
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application has_any ("Salesforce")
| where IPAddress in (IcarusIPs)
   or tostring(RawEventData) has_any ("Klue","Battlecards")
| extend KlueApp = tostring(RawEventData) has_any ("Klue","Battlecards")
| where KlueApp or IPAddress in (IcarusIPs)
| summarize EventCount = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            ActionTypes = make_set(ActionType, 20),
            Objects = make_set(ObjectName, 20),
            UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 10)
          by AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, Application, City, CountryCode
| order by FirstSeen desc
let IcarusIPs = dynamic(["138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(SigninLogs
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where AppDisplayName has_any ("Klue","Battlecards")
      or IPAddress in (IcarusIPs)
 | project TimeGenerated, Type="User", UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, AppId, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, UserAgent, ResultType, ConditionalAccessStatus, Location),
(AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where ServicePrincipalName has_any ("Klue","Battlecards")
      or IPAddress in (IcarusIPs)
 | project TimeGenerated, Type="ServicePrincipal", ServicePrincipalName, AppId, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, ResultType)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Klue Battlecards OAuth App Sign-In From Icarus Extortion IP
id: 9b2e4c1a-6f3d-4d0a-92f1-3e0a5c7b9d4e
description: Sign-in or API activity attributed to the Klue Battlecards connected app originating from one of the four IPs ReliaQuest/Huntress attributed to Icarus during the June 2026 Salesforce data theft campaign.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/klue-oauth-breach-linked-to-icarus-salesforce-data-theft-attacks/
  - https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-integration-abused-in-crm-data-theft
author: thn-usecases
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1528
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1199
logsource:
  product: azure
  service: signinlogs
detection:
  app:
    AppDisplayName|contains:
      - 'Klue'
      - 'Battlecards'
  ip:
    IPAddress:
      - '138.226.246.94'
      - '212.86.125.24'
      - '213.111.148.90'
      - '94.154.32.160'
  condition: app and ip
level: high
(source:azure.activeDirectory OR source:okta) AND (@properties.appDisplayName:(*Klue* OR *Battlecards*) OR @AppDisplayName:(*Klue* OR *Battlecards*)) AND (CIDR(@network.client.ip, 138.226.246.94/32) OR CIDR(@network.client.ip, 212.86.125.24/32) OR CIDR(@network.client.ip, 213.111.148.90/32) OR CIDR(@network.client.ip, 94.154.32.160/32) OR CIDR(@client.ipAddress, 138.226.246.94/32) OR CIDR(@client.ipAddress, 212.86.125.24/32) OR CIDR(@client.ipAddress, 213.111.148.90/32) OR CIDR(@client.ipAddress, 94.154.32.160/32))
#event_simpleName=IdpAuthenticationLog (AppDisplayName=/klue|battlecards/i OR ServicePrincipalName=/klue|battlecards/i OR RemoteAddressIP4=/^(138\.226\.246\.94|212\.86\.125\.24|213\.111\.148\.90|94\.154\.32\.160)$/) | groupBy([UserPrincipal, AppDisplayName, RemoteAddressIP4], function=count())
CLOUD
`salesforce_event_monitoring` (CLIENT_NAME="Klue" OR CLIENT_NAME="Battlecards" OR APPLICATION_NAME="Klue Battlecards" OR CONNECTED_APP_NAME="Klue*") AND (CLIENT_IP="138.226.246.94" OR CLIENT_IP="212.86.125.24" OR CLIENT_IP="213.111.148.90" OR CLIENT_IP="94.154.32.160") | stats count min(_time) as firstSeen max(_time) as lastSeen values(URI) as uris values(USER_ID) as users dc(URI) as distinctEndpoints by CLIENT_IP CONNECTED_APP_NAME | convert ctime(firstSeen) ctime(lastSeen) | sort - count
Salesforce REST API mass /sobjects enumeration via OAuth connected app AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts the reconnaissance phase ReliaQuest documented: an OAuth-authenticated client walking the `/services/data/v59.0/sobjects` endpoint to enumerate available Salesforce objects before deciding what to exfiltrate. The detection is the high distinct-object count per single principal in a short window, regardless of source IP. Rationale: ReliaQuest's blog post explicitly names `/services/data/v59.0/sobjects` as the recon endpoint Icarus walked before exfiltration. Detecting on the endpoint string + per-principal volume catches the unique pre-exfil signature regardless of whether the principal eventually connected from the four published IPs. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-integration-abused-in-crm-data-theft
ATT&CKT1526 T1087.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web Change.Auditing_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Klue/Drift/Outreach/Salesloft sync job doing initial-import schema discovery on a freshly-installed connected app
  • Developer running a Postman/SoqlBuilder script during integration testing
  • Salesforce-native data backup tools (OwnBackup, Spanning) enumerating sobjects nightly
  • DataLoader.io / Workbench bulk schema explore by an admin
Suppression filter
| where ConnectedApp !in~ ("OwnBackup","Spanning Backup","Salesforce Data Loader","Workbench")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify the `CONNECTED_APP_NAME` and `CLIENT_IP` on the bursting principal. If the connected app is Klue Battlecards, escalate immediately per Salesforce's June 2026 advisory. Otherwise, confirm with the owning admin whether a sanctioned data sync was scheduled. 2) Contain: If unsanctioned, revoke the OAuth tokens for that connected app, terminate sessions, and disable the app on the Salesforce tenant. Notify Salesforce Trust if you suspect another vendor compromise. 3) Hunt: Pivot to the same `CLIENT_ID` over the next 24 hours specifically for `/services/data/v59.0/query` bursts (the next attack stage per ReliaQuest) and for any of the four Icarus IPs in the same time window.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application has "Salesforce"
| extend Uri = tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).URI)
| extend ClientId = tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).CLIENT_ID)
| extend ConnectedApp = tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).CONNECTED_APP_NAME)
| where Uri has "/services/data/v59.0/sobjects" or ActivityType has "sobjects"
| summarize ApiCalls = count(),
            DistinctEndpoints = dcount(Uri),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            SampleUris = make_set(Uri, 25)
          by bin(Timestamp, 15m), AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ConnectedApp, ClientId
| where ApiCalls > 50 or DistinctEndpoints > 20
| order by FirstSeen desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor has "Salesforce" or DestinationServiceName has "Salesforce"
| where RequestURL has "/services/data/v59.0/sobjects"
| extend ConnectedApp = coalesce(DeviceCustomString1, RequestClientApplication)
| summarize ApiCalls = count(),
            DistinctEndpoints = dcount(RequestURL),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleUris = make_set(RequestURL, 25)
          by bin(TimeGenerated, 15m), SourceUserName, SourceIP, ConnectedApp
| where ApiCalls > 50 or DistinctEndpoints > 20
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:salesforce @evt.name:(RestApi OR API) AND @uri:*services/data/v59.0/sobjects*
APPLICATION
`salesforce_event_monitoring` URI="*/services/data/v59.0/sobjects*" | bin _time span=15m | stats count dc(URI) as distinct_sobjects values(URI) as sample_uris min(_time) as firstSeen max(_time) as lastSeen by _time CLIENT_IP USER_ID CONNECTED_APP_NAME | where count > 50 OR distinct_sobjects > 20 | convert ctime(firstSeen) ctime(lastSeen) | sort - count
Salesforce /query API burst exfiltration via single OAuth principal AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the data-theft burst ReliaQuest documented: a single OAuth-authenticated principal sending hundreds-to-thousands of REST `/services/data/v59.0/query` calls in a 15-minute window after a preceding slow reconnaissance phase. The 1000-queries-in-15-minutes pattern was explicitly observed by ReliaQuest in at least one victim environment. Rationale: ReliaQuest gave a literal volume signature: '~1,000 queries in a 15-minute window' to `/services/data/v59.0/query`. Threshold of 500/15m + the specific endpoint string is the strongest article-grounded signature for the actual exfil event, distinct from UC3's recon detection. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-integration-abused-in-crm-data-theft • https://www.bankinfosecurity.com/attackers-steal-salesforce-data-from-klue-battlecards-users-a-32011
ATT&CKT1567 T1530 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate analytics tool (Tableau CRM, Snowflake Salesforce connector, Fivetran) doing nightly full-table extract
  • Klue/Drift/Salesloft/Outreach normal sync that batches sObject pulls
  • ERP/MAP integration backfill after a long outage
  • Marketing-ops bulk-segmentation export through DataLoader
Suppression filter
| where ConnectedApp !in~ ("Tableau","Snowflake","Fivetran","Salesforce Data Loader","Mulesoft")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify the bursting OAuth principal/connected app, compare against the tenant's documented sanctioned data-sync schedule, and pull the SObject names being queried — if they include `Account`, `Contact`, `Opportunity`, `Quote`, `Lead`, this matches the Huntress description of stolen data. 2) Contain: Immediately revoke OAuth refresh tokens for the principal, terminate sessions, freeze the connected app, and place the source IP on a tenant block-list. Engage Salesforce Trust if vendor compromise is suspected. 3) Hunt: Look backward 24-48h on the same `CLIENT_ID` for the slower `/services/data/v59.0/sobjects` recon phase (UC3) — ReliaQuest noted the actor 'slowly mapped out their Salesforce objects to identify valuable objects and then rapidly stole data' so the recon usually precedes the burst by hours.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application has "Salesforce"
| extend Uri = tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).URI)
| extend ConnectedApp = tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).CONNECTED_APP_NAME)
| extend RowsReturned = tolong(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).ROW_COUNT)
| where Uri has "/services/data/v59.0/query" or ActivityType has "Query"
| summarize QueryCount = count(),
            DistinctQueries = dcount(Uri),
            TotalRows = sum(RowsReturned),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 5)
          by bin(Timestamp, 15m), AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ConnectedApp
| where QueryCount >= 500 or TotalRows >= 100000
| order by QueryCount desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor has "Salesforce" or DestinationServiceName has "Salesforce"
| where RequestURL has "/services/data/v59.0/query"
| extend ConnectedApp = coalesce(DeviceCustomString1, RequestClientApplication)
| extend RowsReturned = toint(DeviceCustomString2)
| summarize QueryCount = count(),
            DistinctQueries = dcount(RequestURL),
            TotalRows = sum(RowsReturned),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by bin(TimeGenerated, 15m), SourceUserName, SourceIP, ConnectedApp
| where QueryCount >= 500 or TotalRows >= 100000
| order by QueryCount desc
source:salesforce @evt.name:(RestApi OR API) AND @uri:*services/data/v59.0/query*
APPLICATION
`salesforce_event_monitoring` URI="*/services/data/v59.0/query*" | bin _time span=15m | stats count as queryCount dc(URI) as distinctQueries sum(ROW_COUNT) as totalRows values(USER_ID) as users by _time CLIENT_IP CONNECTED_APP_NAME USER_ID | where queryCount >= 500 OR totalRows >= 100000 | sort - queryCount
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |
    User-driven consent to a third-party OAuth application — illicit-
    consent attack precursor. Pair with first-time-seen-app heuristic
    in your SIEM for higher fidelity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1528
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    product: azure
    service: auditlogs
detection:
    selection:
        OperationName: 'Consent to application'
        Result: 'success'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate first-time SaaS app onboarding
level: medium
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.

DeviceProcessEvents

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f

detection:

INC ransomware BYOVD vulnerable filter-driver load (filwfp.sys / filnk.sys / fildds.sys) AIInstallation High
Detects load or install of the three vulnerable filter-system drivers (filwfp.sys, filnk.sys, fildds.sys) that INC ransomware affiliates abuse via BYOVD to impair Defender/EDR before encryption. These driver names are highly article-specific and not common in legitimate enterprise software. Rationale: filwfp.sys, filnk.sys, fildds.sys are three specific vulnerable drivers explicitly named in the Acronis writeup as INC's BYOVD toolkit. None are part of any mainstream commercial product, so any load is high-fidelity.
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher reproducing the BYOVD chain in a malware-analysis VM
  • Red-team engagement using a leaked INC affiliate toolkit
  • Backup/storage product that legitimately ships one of these driver names (verify the SHA256 against vendor catalogue first)
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe", "MsSense.exe")) and not(FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\System32\drivers\" and InitiatingProcessAccountName == "system" and InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "services.exe" and SHA256 in (dynamic([])))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull SHA256 of the loaded .sys, look up signer/age; check whether host has a paired Defender 'Impair Defenses' or service-stop alert in the prior 15 minutes. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the device via Defender Live Response; capture memory image before reboot; block driver hash tenant-wide via Defender ASR vulnerable-driver list (or WDAC) and quarantine the .sys file. 3) HUNT: Pivot on InitiatingProcessFolderPath for parent dropper, then search for ScreenConnect/AnyDesk/TeamViewer installs, rclone.exe activity, and access to Veeam backup shares from the same host in the prior 24h to find the affiliate's full chain.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("DriverLoad", "AsrVulnerableSignedDriverAudited", "AsrVulnerableSignedDriverBlocked")
| where FileName in~ ("filwfp.sys", "filnk.sys", "fildds.sys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 6
| where ParameterXml has_any ("filwfp.sys", "filnk.sys", "fildds.sys")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventID, ParameterXml
| order by TimeGenerated desc

INC Rust encryptor invoked with --esxi VM-shutdown flag AIActions on Objectives High
Detects any process execution carrying the '--esxi' command-line argument, which is the documented INC ransomware Rust encryptor switch that shuts down virtual machines before encryption on Linux/ESXi hosts (and observed on Windows when staged from a jump box). This argument is not a standard flag for any benign Windows utility. Rationale: '--esxi' is explicitly called out as INC's encryptor argument that triggers VM shutdown. The token is highly unusual in normal command-line traffic — no Microsoft, VMware, or RMM utility uses it natively.
ATT&CKT1486 T1489
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal IR/purple-team exercise running a captured INC sample in a lab subnet
  • VMware/ESXi admin scripts that happen to pass '--esxi' as a custom argument to in-house tooling
  • Security testing of the YARA/sandbox pipeline replaying INC payload metadata
Suppression filter
| where not(FolderPath has_any (@"\IR-Sandbox\", @"\malware-analysis\")) and not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe") and FolderPath startswith @"C:\Tools\IR\")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and SHA256; correlate to any vssadmin/wmic shadow-copy deletion, BYOVD driver load, or RMM tool install on the same host in the prior 60 minutes. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host immediately via EDR network containment; snapshot the system; if multiple hosts hit simultaneously, declare incident and block the binary hash tenant-wide. 3) HUNT: Search for the same binary SHA256 across the estate, look for rclone exfil and 7-Zip/WinRAR archive staging on file servers, and enumerate VMware/ESXi management VLAN authentications from compromised credentials in the last 7 days.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--esxi"
| where not(AccountName endswith "$")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "--esxi"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
